result.summary: Eteocles, anxious over his failed ambush, learns that only Maeon survived; Maeon kills himself defying the king, and Thebes mourns its dead. Jupiter sends Mars to stir Argos to war while Tydeus returns and inflames the Argives. The seers read dire omens, Capaneus mocks them, and Argia pleads with Adrastus to grant war for Polynices.

scenes.title: Eteocles waits; Maeon returns
scenes.summary: Eteocles frets through the night over the ambush. At dawn Maeon returns alone, and the Theban mothers wail.
scenes.stakes: Eteocles risks the failure of his plot and its exposure; Maeon returns in grief as sole survivor.

scenes.title: Maeon's defiance and death
scenes.summary: Maeon reports the slaughter, curses the king, and kills himself before Eteocles' guards can seize him. The poet praises him.
scenes.stakes: Maeon faces death at the king's hands and chooses to die free.

scenes.title: Thebes mourns the slain
scenes.summary: The Thebans go to the ambush site, search the corpses and lament; Ide mourns her twin sons. Aletes compares the grief to earlier Theban woes and curses Eteocles.
scenes.stakes: Grieving families and Aletes face further war and ruin.

scenes.title: Jupiter sends Mars to war
scenes.summary: Jupiter commands Mars to rouse Argos and warns the other gods not to interfere. Venus pleads for Thebes, but Mars says the Fates compel him.
scenes.stakes: Venus fears for her Theban descendants; Mars risks Jupiter's wrath if he disobeys.

scenes.title: Tydeus rouses Argos
scenes.summary: Tydeus returns wounded and calls for war. Polynices feigns reluctance, and Adrastus counsels patience while Tydeus is tended.
scenes.stakes: Polynices' claim to the throne and Argos' peace hang in the balance.

scenes.title: Night and Mars's progress
scenes.summary: Sunset yields to night, and Mars drives through Greece, spreading war-fever with Rumour and Panic.

scenes.title: The seers read the omens
scenes.summary: Adrastus sends Amphiaraus and Melampus to seek omens on Mount Aphesas. They see birds killing each other, foretelling doom, and Amphiaraus returns grieved.
scenes.stakes: Amphiaraus foresees his own death and the destruction of the Argive host.

scenes.title: Capaneus defies Amphiaraus
scenes.summary: Argos arms itself, and the crowd demands war. Capaneus scorns prophecy; Amphiaraus warns them and foretells his doom, but the crowd cheers Capaneus.
scenes.stakes: The Argives risk ruin by ignoring divine warnings; Amphiaraus faces fated death.

scenes.title: Argia pleads with Adrastus
scenes.summary: Argia visits her father at night and begs him to grant war for her husband. Adrastus promises help in due time.
scenes.stakes: Argia risks her husband's despair and her child's future as an exile's heir.

alias_notes.explanation: Epithet of Apollo, used to address Amphiaraus as his follower.
Argive king, called after Perseus, Argos' hero.

notable_quotes.reason: Capaneus's famous impious claim that fear first created the gods.
Capaneus declares valour and sword his only gods.
Narrator's reflection on humanity's craving to know the future.

analysis.text: Human choice and divine compulsion collide: Jupiter and the Fates ordain war while mortals rush into it, ignoring omens.
Capaneus's contempt for prophecy contrasts with Amphiaraus's grim knowledge, showing impiety and foresight in opposition.

legacy.text: Capaneus's line that fear made the gods echoes a saying often attributed to Statius, and was quoted by later writers on religion.

fun_facts.text: Statius wrote the Thebaid in the late first century AD, and Dante later placed Capaneus in Hell.

language_notes.text: "Aonian" means Boeotian, the region around Thebes; Aonia was a poetic name for it, so the palace is Eteocles' at Thebes.
Gradivus is a title of Mars, god of war (the Greek Ares), invoked here as a patron of warriors.
"I ween" is archaic for "I think" or "I suppose"; "adamant" is a legendary unbreakable metal.
The Olenian star is Capella, the Goat, whose rising was associated with storms; it tempted the helmsman to sail, as hope has tempted Eteocles.
"Agenorean" means Theban, from Agenor, father of Cadmus, who founded Thebes; "Lucifer" is the morning star.
Tethys, a sea goddess, and Hyperion, a sun god, stand for the sea and the rising sun; the poet means dawn is breaking.
"The son of Haemon" is Maeon, the sole survivor of the ambush. The note [2] marks the translator's identification.
"Audience at his desire" means Maeon asked for a hearing and the king allowed it. "Hapless life" is Maeon's own life, spared by Tydeus.
Maeon calls himself the "evil omen" the king must receive. The "cruel grace" is his survival, which he refuses to credit to pleading or trickery.
Atropos is the Fate who cuts the thread of life. Maeon says she and destiny spared him until now.
"Fifty spirits" are the fifty Theban ambushers slain by Tydeus. "Plaint" means lament. "I also delay not" announces his coming suicide.
"Truculent" means fierce and aggressive. "Dallied" means lingered or hesitated.
Dodona and the "Cirrhaean virgin" (the Pythia at Delphi, near Cirrha) are oracles of Jove and Apollo. Their prophecy will go on while Phoebus (Apollo) stays silent.
"Ogygiana" means Theban, from Ogyges, a legendary early king of Thebes. Maeon's soul is sent to Elysium, away from Thebes' tyrant.
The 'infamous rocks' and 'accursed wood' are the ambush site, where fifty Theban warriors were killed by Tydeus, so they are tainted by that crime.
Thessalian witches were proverbial in antiquity for necromancy and for raising or manipulating the dead.
Avernus' sire means Pluto, lord of the underworld, named after the lake Avernus, an entrance to the realm of the dead.
Ogygia here means Thebes, after the legendary early king Ogyges; it is not Calypso's island.
Lucina is the Roman goddess who presided over childbirth.
The Sidonian wanderer is Cadmus, who sowed dragon's teeth at Thebes; armed men sprang up from them. Aonia is Boeotia.
Athamas, driven mad by Juno, hunted his son Learchus as a wild beast; Agave, in Bacchic frenzy, killed her son Pentheus.
The Tantalid is Niobe, daughter of Tantalus, whose children were slain by Apollo and Diana after she boasted against Latona.
Actaeon spied on Diana (Delia) bathing and was turned into a stag, killed by his own hounds. The queen is Niobe, turned to stone and weeping.
Gradivus is a title of Mars, the war god, often translated as 'the marching one'.
The Bistonians and Getae were Thracian peoples; Thrace was traditionally Mars's homeland and favourite haunt.
The Fates spin and cut the thread of destiny; 'dark spindles of the Sisters' means their decrees, which even Jupiter says he must obey.
The 'Lemnian chains' recall Vulcan trapping Venus and Mars in a net on Lemnos after discovering their adultery.
'Guerdon' is an archaic word for reward.
The 'beloved daughter' is Harmonia, child of Venus and Mars, married to Cadmus, the Tyrian founder of Thebes; the marriage brought a doom on their line.
Harmonia and Cadmus were later turned into serpents, hence the daughter crawling and spewing poison on Illyrian grass.
Mars's 'uncle' is Pluto, ruler of the underworld, brother of Jupiter.
Othrys and Ossa are Thessalian mountains, here pictured as Jupiter's perches for hurling thunderbolts.
Danaan means Argive, from Danaus, legendary ancestor of the Argives; Prosymna is a district near Argos.
Echionian means Theban, from Echion, one of the Sown Men who sprang from the dragon's teeth at Thebes.
The Lord of Arms is Mars, god of war; the phrase means the war god predisposes them to believe everything.
Lerna is a marsh near Argos; 'ruler of Lerna' means Adrastus, king of Argos.
The Bebrycian warden is Amycus, a savage king who forced strangers to box and killed them; the Sauromatae were a wild northern people.
Sons of Inachus means the Argives, from Inachus, the first river-god and king of Argos; the Cadmean hero is Polynices, of Cadmus's Thebes.
Maeon was the Theban whom Tydeus spared from the ambush so that he could carry the news home.
Tyrian exile is Polynices, whose ancestor Cadmus came from Tyre in Phoenicia.
The Sun's chariot is unyoked in Ocean each evening; Nereus is a sea-god, father of the sea-nymphs, and the Hours are goddesses of the seasons who attend the Sun.
Labdacian prince means Polynices, descendant of Labdacus, an earlier king of Thebes.
The Persean hero is Adrastus, king of Argos, whose city was linked to Perseus, its legendary hero.
Cirrha's waters refer to the Delphic Apollo's sacred springs near Cirrha; drinking them stands for prophetic inspiration.
Lists famous oracles: Hammon in Libya, Lycia's Apollo, the Egyptian bull Apis, Branchus's oracle at Didyma, Dodona's oaks. All are said to be less certain than bird omens.
Thunder on the left was a favourable sign in this Roman augury tradition. Echionian means Theban, from Echion, one of the Sown Men.
Minerva's bird is the owl; the 'dark companion of the tripod' is probably the raven, Apollo's bird. The bearer of the thunderbolt is Jupiter's eagle.
The seer abruptly addresses the failing wings, as the fall of Argive champions is foreshadowed in the birds' deaths.
Clotho is the Fate who spins the thread of life.
Melampus is the legendary seer, Amphiaraus' ancestor; the poet addresses him, suggesting the seer's line shares the shame of unwelcome prophecy.
The Thunderer is Jove; his 'behests' are the decrees driving Argos to war.
Gortynian: from Gortyn in Crete, famed for archers and bows.
Pholoe's forests were home of the Centaurs; Aetnaean brethren are the Cyclopes. Both comparisons make Capaneus a savage giant.
Inachus was the river-god and first king of Argos; 'sons of Inachus' means Argives.
Cirrha's height is Delphi, Apollo's oracle, where a virgin priestess (Pythia) delivered obscure riddling answers.
Oeclides: son of Oecles, i.e. Amphiaraus.
Thymbraean is Apollo, from his shrine at Thymbra. Megaera is a Fury; Lachesis is the Fate who measures out life's thread.
Tyrrhenian clangour means the war trumpet, said to be an Etruscan invention.
Sidonian foe means the Thebans, descendants of Cadmus, who came from Phoenician Sidon. The chaplets are the priest's sacred garlands.
Arctos is the Great Bear constellation, which never sets below the horizon, so it alone 'survives' as other stars sink into the ocean at dawn.
Hymen is the god of marriage; Juno presided over marriage. Their torches at Argia's wedding were ill-omened, hinting at the troubles that followed.
'Grant war' means to authorize and support a military expedition to restore Polynices to his throne in Thebes.
Apollo's oracle told Adrastus that his daughters would marry a boar and a lion, which he took to mean the exiles Polynices and Tydeus.
Casques are helmets; clarions are shrill war trumpets.

context_notes.text: Eteocles, king of Thebes, has broken the agreed alternation of rule with his brother Polynices and sent fifty men to ambush Tydeus, Polynices' envoy, on his way home.
Cithaeron is the mountain near Thebes, famous in Theban myth. Thebes was known for its seven gates.
The "mothers" are Theban women who fear their sons were among the fifty ambushers; Maeon's solitary return tells them all are lost.
Maeon is the one Theban ambusher whom Tydeus spared so he could carry word home. The "hated king" is Eteocles, who has barred his brother Polynices from the throne.
Phlegyas and Labdacus are Eteocles' henchmen, here acting as his military enforcers.
Denying cremation and burial was a grave impiety, since the unburied dead could not find rest among the shades.
Ide is the mother of the twins Phegeus and Idas, both killed in the ambush.
Chthonius, Pentheus, Phaedimus, Phylleus and Acamas are Theban warriors killed in the ambush; their families mourn them.
The Sisters are the Fates, who spin and fix each person's destiny, with Jove's approval.
The cruel monarch is Eteocles, who broke the agreement to share the throne with his brother Polynices and ordered the ambush on Tydeus.
Tydeus, an Argive champion, was ambushed by Theban men on his embassy to Thebes and killed them all but one; he now returns to Argos.
Jupiter swears by the Styx-like Elysian streams; oaths by sacred waters were binding on gods. Juno favoured Argos, so her protecting Thebes would be surprising.
Tydeus, an exile from Calydon, was sent by Adrastus to Thebes to demand that Eteocles yield the throne to Polynices; he killed fifty ambushers on the way back.
Polynices and Tydeus both married daughters of Adrastus, so the 'spouse' and 'her father' are Argia and Adrastus.
Idmon is an Argive healer, here called Epidaurian after Epidaurus, a city famed for healing.
Mars, god of war, rouses the regions of Greece, Arcadia and Laconia, to prepare for the coming conflict.
Amphiaraus and Melampus are famed Argive seers; Melampus was a legendary prophet and Amphiaraus is destined to die in the war.
Perseus, the legendary hero of Argos, flew on winged sandals; his mother Danae watched him.
Melampus recalls sailing with Jason on the Argo; Mopsus was the Argonauts' seer.
Amphiaraus is the Argive prophet who has seen in the omens that the expedition against Thebes will fail, and that he will die.
Enceladus was a giant buried beneath Etna by the gods; his shifting was said to cause eruptions. Pelorus is the Sicilian cape near it.
Tydeus, an Argive envoy, was ambushed by Thebans on his way home; this breach of covenant is the pretext for war.
Argia is daughter of Adrastus, king of Argos, and wife of the exiled Polynices. Thessander is their infant son.
Adrastus is old and wary; he hesitates to commit Argos to war, and the realm's succession and governance are unsettled.

literary_notes.text: Care "holds vigil" and fear "broods" like living figures, turning Eteocles' guilty anxiety into active tormentors.
Eteocles scorns Tydeus as easy prey, while the reader knows from earlier events that Tydeus is formidable and the ambush will fail.
Eteocles is compared to a helmsman lured from a safe harbour into a storm; he is carried by events he cannot reverse.
Maeon's wailing and beaten breast reveal the disaster before any words, building suspense.
The herdsman who finds his herd slaughtered parallels Maeon, the lone survivor, who must tell the king of his lost companions.
The mothers' cry is likened to a captured city or a sinking ship, conveying total catastrophe.
Maeon turns to address the stars, his dead comrades and the king in turn. The shift gives his speech the force of a solemn oath.
The curse of haunting spirits and unholy war foretells the doom of Eteocles and Thebes. The last clause also points to Maeon's suicide.
His speech breaks off mid-curse as the sword enters his side, so the action cuts the words short.
The poet addresses the dead Maeon directly and asks how to praise him enough. This lifts him into heroic memory.
Grief is made a figure with bloody torn clothes and pierced breast, goading the mothers into mourning.
Ide's frantic search among the corpses is compared to a Thessalian witch hunting a body at night with her torch.
Ide's anguished questions to her dead sons convey her grief in broken, emotional speech.
The sons, whom she hoped would win fame, die obscure and unpraised, reversing the glory she expected.
Aletes places the present grief within Thebes' long history of mythic disasters, beginning with Cadmus' sowing of the dragon's teeth.
The narrator explains Aletes' boldness by his age and nearness to death, commenting on his motive.
Lightning, blood-red glow and monstrous shield figures make Mars's arrival vivid and terrifying, even rivalling the sun.
The gods' sudden silence is compared to a windless, motionless summer landscape, stressing how Jupiter's command stills all resistance.
Venus says even the husband she wronged obeys her, bitterly contrasting Vulcan's loyalty with Mars's refusal.
Mars addresses Venus with tender titles, showing the fierce war god softened by love before he yields to fate.
Mars's swift descent is likened to Jupiter's thunderbolt, a bearer of divine command and omen of disaster.
Tydeus is compared to a victorious bull, bloodied but proud; the beast's swelling pride mirrors the hero's, and the beaten foe parallels the slain Thebans.
Rumour is pictured as a living force that doubles fear once it is welcomed, while Mars actively sways minds.
Tydeus likens himself to a fortified tower under siege, magnifying his courage and the scale of the ambush.
Polynices' show of reluctance is called dissembling: he pretends to spare Argos while actually fanning its eagerness for war.
Fury, Wrath and Panic act as Mars's attendants, making war's emotions into servants of the god.
Neptune driving the winds is likened to Mars driving Rumour, enlarging the war-god's march through an epic comparison.
The ring of swans stands for Thebes, the sevenfold attackers for the Argive chiefs, making the omen an allegory.
Amphiaraus recognises his own fall in the dying bird, signalling his death in the war.
The narrator suddenly questions the human desire to know the future, a moralising digression on prophecy.
The golden age is contrasted with present corruption, a classical motif of decline from innocence.
The roar of the crowd is compared to the sea and a volcano's eruption, conveying vast, uncontrollable force.
Capaneus is introduced as noble yet impious, contemptuous of gods and reckless of life, marking him as proud and doomed.
A rush of questions shows Amphiaraus' anguish and tries to shame the crowd into reflection.
Capaneus' bold, compressed claim that fear made the gods sums up his atheism.
The flooding torrent likens the crowd's fury to a natural force that is stopped only when night falls.
The Bear's wagon 'envies' the fleeing stars, giving the constellation human feeling while marking the hour before dawn.
Argia says even a tigress or a heart harder than shore rocks could not endure her husband's weeping, stressing her compassion.
The repeated address 'thou knowest not, good father' makes her plea more emotional and intimate.
Adrastus's cares calling him away, with the vague promise of delay, hints that war will come but only after hesitation.
